messages.subject: Re: [knitr] highlight style for jss
messages.body_plain:
I used syntax highlighting once in a JSS submission, and the editors
said it was not allowed. You might try again, but I guess you are
likely to fail again like me. If you use knitr for JSS articles, the
only "correct" thing to do is to use the Sweave style, which can be
obtained via knitr::render_sweave() in the first code chunk, e.g.

<<setup, include=FALSE>>=
knitr::render_sweave()
@

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Bad behavior when passing code chunks through macros
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Bad behavior when passing code chunks through macros
messages.body_plain:
Sounds like a pure LaTeX question. If that is the case, sorry I cannot
help. There is no way for R or knitr to detect whether the PDF output
is mis-formatted or not. I do not think it is even possible for LaTeX
or any other tools to do so, because it is nearly impossible to define
what the expected format is via code, unless you read and parse PDF,
which I imagine will be a very painful job to do (at least I have no
idea how to do it).

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

On Fri, Nov 7, 2014 at 6:51 AM, Justace Clutter <just...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Knitrs...
>
> I have come across a situation where I was passing a code chunk through a macro that I defined in an Rnw file.  When I generated the PDF file, all of my properly indented code was compactified into a very long single line of code.  After some research I determined that the knitr package is wrapping all of the code blocks inside an alltt environment (reasonable).  Unfortunately, passing chunks of latex code wrapped in an alltt environment through a macro argument kills its formatting.  A simple example is presented below:
>
> \documentclass{article}
>
>
> \newcommand{\myfunction}[1]{#1}
>
>
> \begin{document}
>
>
> \begin{alltt}
> This
> is a test
> again
> \end{alltt}
>
>
> \myfunction{
> \begin{alltt}
> This
> is a test
> again
> \end{alltt}
> }
>
>
> \end{document}
>
> The resulting document looks like the following:
>

> As you can see, the text in the first block is as it was supposed to be while the text in the second block has lost its manual formatting.  This question has been addressed on stack exchange at http://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/63095/problem-with-alltt-package-when-defining-new-command.
>
> Is there some way to alert the user runtime that the code blocks will be miss-formed when passing as a macro argument.  I know this might seem like an edge case but I spent a larger chunk of time last night trying to figure this out.  I am hopeful that others will not need to spend that time.
>

messages.subject: chunk option 'size' fails when using packages beamer and beamerposter
messages.subject_clean: chunk option 'size' fails when using packages beamer and beamerposter
messages.body_plain:
Dear knitrs,

I am writing a conference poster with knitr, beamer and beamerposter and I am faced with the problem that by loading the beamerposter package in the preamble of my document I cannot any longer control font size via the chunk option (neither globally nor locally). However, when I compile the same document without the beamer poster package, font size is rendered just as it should. I haven't noticed any differences between the *.tex files in both cases and I wonder where to start to tackle this issue.

You can reproduce the failure with the code below, either compiling with or without the beamer poster package.

Thanks for any insight into the problem,
Nelson

\documentclass{beamer}
%\usepackage[scale=1]{beamerposter}
\begin{document}

<<setup, include=FALSE>>=
library(knitr)
opts_chunk$set(
concordance=TRUE,
size="tiny"
)
@

\begin{frame}[fragile]
This text is normal-sized.

<<boring-random>>=
cat("This should be tiny.")
@
\end{frame}
\end{document}

\include{diff_slum}

\documentclass[]{article}
\setlength{\pdfpagewidth}{8.5in} \setlength{\pdfpageheight}{11in}
\begin{document}

and

\end{document}

from your included file.

I preparing some R tutorials and I would like to add some code in my text. This code is not meant to be run, but only to show. For longer code section, I can use the option eval=FALSE but I'm not sure if there is a way to do it with inline code. For example, I would like to do something like:

We used the function ''plot()'' to produce ....

I have seen some documents where the ''plot()'' would appears in a small box with colours to emphasis the code or the function. Is it done with LaTeX commands?

Thank you in advance,
Philippe

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to create a document that demonstrates how axis() can be used to add axis labels to an existing plot.  I was hoping to create a plot and, using fig.show='hold',  have that same plot shown next to the original plot but followed with axis() to add the new axis labels.  For example, I have the following chunk.

<<bad, fig.height=2, fig.width=2, fig.show='hold'>>=
par(mar=c(3,3,0.5,0.5),mgp=c(1.8,0.65,0))
tmp <- rnorm(100)
plot(tmp)
plot(tmp)
axis(1,c(20,60,100))
@

However, this simply produces one plot with the additional axis labels (i.e., the last plot produced).

If the two calls to plot() have different data then I get the side-by-side plots.

<<good1, fig.height=2, fig.width=2, fig.show='hold'>>=
par(mar=c(3,3,0.5,0.5),mgp=c(1.8,0.65,0))
plot(rnorm(100))
plot(rnorm(100))
axis(1,c(20,60,100))
@

I know that I can get my desired side-by-side plots by including mfrow=c(1,2) in par() (shown below), but I am wondering if there is a knitr solution to my issue (rather than using par()).

<<good2, fig.height=2, fig.width=4,fig.show='hold'>>=
par(mar=c(3,3,0.5,0.5),mgp=c(1.8,0.65,0),mfrow=c(1,2))
tmp <- rnorm(100)
plot(tmp)
plot(tmp)
axis(1,c(20,60,100))
@

p.s., I am using knitr v1.8, R v3.1.1, Rstudio 0.98.1062, and Windows.  The entire minimal example of the code above is shown below.

\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}

I would like the plot repeated so I can demonstrate adding axis values.

<<bad, fig.height=2, fig.width=2, fig.show='hold'>>=
par(mar=c(3,3,0.5,0.5),mgp=c(1.8,0.65,0))

@

<<good1, fig.height=2, fig.width=2, fig.show='hold'>>=

plot(rnorm(100))
axis(1,c(20,60,100))

<<good2, fig.height=2, fig.width=4,fig.show='hold'>>=

plot(tmp)
plot(tmp)
axis(1,c(20,60,100))
@

Unfortunately that is by design. Identical plots in the same code
chunk are removed. However, I do not see why you have to draw
identical plots. If you want to show a plot, then some new elements
added to the plot, you can keep the full history by fig.keep = 'all',
e.g.

<<fig.height=2, fig.width=2, fig.show='hold', fig.keep='all'>>=

par(mar=c(3,3,0.5,0.5),mgp=c(1.8,0.65,0))
tmp <- rnorm(100)
plot(tmp)

axis(1,c(20,60,100))
@

This code chunk will generate two plots.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

messages.body_plain:
I realized the previous solution was no longer valid. With the latest
version of knitr, you should use

knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  sub('\\usepackage[]{color}', '\\usepackage{xcolor}', x, fixed = TRUE)
})

I have attached a minimal example, and please read FAQ 1 before you
report more issues: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/FAQ.md

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name
